cues.text: A Noble Canon
Born in 1651 at Reims into an old and distinguished French family, John Baptist was ordained a priest.
He held a comfortable position as a cathedral canon before becoming, almost accidentally, involved in educating poor children through his support for struggling lay schoolteachers in Reims.
Descending from Privilege
As his involvement deepened, John Baptist made increasingly radical choices: he invited the schoolteachers to live in his family home and resigned his lucrative canonry.
Eventually, during a famine, he distributed his entire personal fortune to the poor.

He took these steps gradually and deliberately, aware they would strip away every social advantage his birth had given him, placing himself on equal footing with the humble teachers he had come to lead.
Founding the Christian Brothers
John Baptist organized his teachers into a religious community of laymen — deliberately not ordained priests — dedicated entirely to teaching, called the Brothers of the Christian Schools .

He developed a comprehensive, structured pedagogical method emphasizing whole-class instruction in the vernacular French rather than Latin, a significant innovation for an era when education for the poor, where it existed at all, was haphazard and inconsistent.
Founding the First Teacher Training College
Recognizing that his method could only spread as far as properly trained teachers were available, John Baptist established an institution for training lay teachers.
Many historians regard it as the first true 'normal school', predating similar institutions in Germany by decades.
He also founded, in 1699, the Christian Academy of Paris, an early form of adult Sunday school offering practical subjects like geometry and architecture alongside religious instruction.
Perseverance Through Opposition

De la Salle's schools, offering quality education entirely without charge, drew resentment from established fee-charging schoolmasters who saw their livelihoods threatened, and he faced years of legal and social opposition as a result.
He nonetheless steadily expanded his institute's reach across France, insisting throughout on his own rule that no school be staffed by fewer than two Brothers working together.
Legacy

John Baptist died at Saint-Yon, near Rouen, on Good Friday 1719, having lived to see a formally elected successor take charge of his institute according to rules he had carefully established during his lifetime.
Canonized in 1900 and declared patron of teachers by Pope Pius XII in 1950, he remains honored by the Church.
Over three centuries later, his Brothers of the Christian Schools remain one of the largest teaching orders in the Catholic Church.
They still operate schools worldwide according to the essential principles he first developed in Reims.
